# Androgens

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Endocrinology > Basics of endocrinology and metabolism > Androgens*

[Original Article Link](/library/pH0Lrh)

---

## Summary

Androgens (male sex <u>hormones</u>) play a key role in the development and function of the <u>male reproductive system</u>. They are furthermore responsible for the development of <u>skeletal muscle</u> mass, <u>bone density</u>, and <u>erythropoiesis</u>. <u>Testosterone</u> is the main <u>androgen</u> and <u>anabolic steroid</u> in male individuals, in whom it is secreted primarily by <u>Leydig cells</u> in the <u>testicles</u>. In female individuals, <u>testosterone</u> acts as an <u>estrogen</u> precursor and is secreted by theca <u>interstitial</u> cells in the <u>ovaries</u>. Other androgens include <u>androstenedione</u> and <u>dehydroepiandrosterone</u> (<u>DHEA</u>), which are secreted in the <u>adrenal cortex</u>. The production of androgens is controlled by the <u>hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis</u> (<u>HPG axis</u>), whose function can be impaired by a deficiency or excess of <u>testosterone</u>. The clinical manifestations of these dysfunctions depend on the stage of development in which the imbalance occurs. <u>Testosterone</u> deficiency during <u>embryonic development</u> leads to the feminization of the male external genitalia. In the prepubescent phase, it can cause <u>hypogonadism</u> and <u>delayed puberty</u> associated with delayed constitutional growth. After <u>puberty</u>, <u>testosterone</u> deficiency can cause <u>infertility</u>. Synthetic androgens (<u>anabolic</u>-androgenic <u>steroids</u>) are used to treat the effects of <u>testosterone</u> deficiency (e.g., <u>delayed puberty</u>) and diseases associated with muscle loss (e.g., cancer, <u>acquired immunodeficiency syndrome</u>). Long-term effects of <u>anabolic</u>-androgenic <u>steroids</u>, frequently seen in individuals who misuse them to promote muscle growth, include <u>liver</u> and <u>kidney</u> damage, <u>cardiomegaly</u>, behavioral changes (e.g., <u>paranoia</u>, aggression), and <u>hypogonadism</u>.




For more information on androgens and their clinical relevance, see the articles on “<u>General endocrinology</u>,” "<u>Adrenal gland</u>,” “<u>Male reproductive organs</u>,” “<u>Differences (disorders) of sex development</u>,” and “<u>Development of the reproductive system</u>.”

## Overview of androgen synthesis

### <u>Testosterone</u> synthesis




<u>Testosterone</u> synthesis takes place in the <u>testicles</u>.




* The <u>hypothalamus</u> secretes <u>gonadotropin-releasing hormone</u> (<u>GnRH</u>) in pulses.

* <u>GnRH</u> stimulates the <u>anterior pituitary</u> cells to secrete <u>luteinizing hormone</u> (<u>LH</u>) and <u>follicle-stimulating hormone</u> (<u>FSH</u>).

* <u>LH</u> stimulates <u>Leydig cells</u> to produce <u>testosterone</u>.

* <u>FSH</u> stimulates <u>Sertoli cells</u> to release:

* <u>Androgen</u>-binding protein, stimulating <u>spermatogenesis</u>

* <u>Inhibin B</u>: Serves as negative feedback control for <u>FSH</u> secretion, a marker of <u>Sertoli cell</u> function and of <u>spermatogenesis</u>.





![Hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis (male)](media/eg2nh4n5amj7ctt5g2b8gip1.jpg)

Hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis (male)




### <u>Adrenal</u> <u>androgen synthesis</u>




Although the majority of <u>testosterone</u> is produced by the <u>Leydig cells</u> in the <u>testicles</u>, the <u>adrenal cortex</u> contributes to <u>androgen</u> production as well.




* A stimulus triggers the secretion of <u>CRH</u>, leading to increased secretion of <u>ACTH</u> by the <u>pituitary gland</u>.

* <u>ACTH</u> stimulates the conversion of <u>cholesterol</u> into <u>pregnenolone</u> in the <u>adrenal cortex</u>.

* Enzymatic pathways trigger <u>DHEA</u> and <u>androstenedione</u> production in the <u>zona reticularis</u>.

* <u>Androstenedione</u> is converted into <u>testosterone</u>, which is then transformed into <u>dihydrotestosterone</u> via <u>5α-reductase</u>.

* <u>Aromatase</u> converts <u>testosterone</u> into <u>estradiol</u> and <u>androstenedione</u>, which is then transformed into <u>estrone</u>.





![Hormonal feedback control of the adrenal hormones](media/kmx2ih7vk3weibkheza0suyf.jpg)

Hormonal feedback control of the adrenal hormones

![Biosynthesis of adrenal steroid hormones](media/m7fmxa166ry7sacx3qstt8ur.jpg)

Biosynthesis of adrenal steroid hormones




### Feedback control mechanisms




* Central regulation: The release of <u>GnRH</u> during <u>puberty</u> stimulates the secretion of <u>FSH</u>, <u>LH</u>, and sex <u>hormones</u>.

* Peripheral regulation: via feedback inhibition of <u>GnRH</u>, <u>FSH</u>, and <u>LH</u> secretion by androgens and <u>inhibin</u>

* <u>Sex hormone-binding globulins</u> (SHBGs)

* Involved in the transport of sex <u>steroids</u> in plasma

* <u>Testosterone:SHBG ratio</u>

* Correlates with values of free <u>testosterone</u>

* Used to assess for <u>hyperandrogenism</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>testosterone</u> and <u>estrogen</u> precursors <u>DHEA</u> and <u>androstenedione</u> are produced in the <u>adrenal cortex</u> in both male and female individuals. <u>Testosterone</u> is produced by <u>Leydig cells</u> in the <u>testicles</u> and, to a lesser degree, by the theca <u>interstitial</u> cells in the <u>ovaries</u>.




> [!NOTE]
> AnDRostenedione is produced by the <u>ADR</u>enal glands and TESTostetone by the TESTicles.

## Anabolic–androgenic steroids

* Definition: synthetic derivatives of <u>testosterone</u>

* Indications

* <u>Primary hypogonadism</u>, <u>delayed puberty</u> in boys, <u>hypogonadotropic hypogonadism</u>, <u>gonadotropin</u> and <u>luteinizing hormone</u>-<u>releasing hormone</u> deficiency, <u>pituitary</u>-<u>hypothalamic</u> axis dysfunction, muscle mass loss in cancer and <u>acquired immunodeficiency syndrome</u>

* <u>Anabolic steroids</u> are sometimes misused as performance-enhancing drugs by athletes.

* Mechanism of action: activate <u>androgen</u> <u>receptors</u>

* Side effects

* Behavioral changes: aggressive behavior

* Cardiovascular: <u>coronary heart disease</u>, <u>cardiomyopathy</u>, <u>hypertension</u>, <u>stroke</u>, <u>dyslipidemia</u> (↑ <u>LDL</u>, ↓ <u>HDL</u>)

* Hepatic: <u>cholestatic jaundice</u>, hepatic <u>neoplasms</u>, cysts

* Renal: <u>kidney failure</u>

* Infections (from sharing needles in misuse): <u>HIV</u>, <u>hepatitis B</u>

* Dermatological: <u>acne</u>

* Hematologic: ↑ <u>hemoglobin</u> and <u>hematocrit</u>

* Musculoskeletal: <u>tendon</u> rupture, premature bone maturation and closure of <u>epiphyseal plates</u>

* Female-specific

* <u>Virilization</u>: <u>hirsutism</u>, male-pattern baldness, <u>breast atrophy</u>, voice deepening

* Irregular <u>menses</u>

* Male-specific

* <u>Gynecomastia</u>

* Decreased testicular size

* Decreased <u>sperm</u> count, <u>azoospermia</u>

* Decreased libido, <u>erectile dysfunction</u>, <u>infertility</u>

* <u>Prostatic</u> <u>hypertrophy</u>

## Clinical significance of androgens

* <u>Hyperandrogenism</u>

* <u>Congenital adrenal hyperplasia</u>

* <u>Androgen</u>-secreting tumors

* <u>17α-hydroxylase deficiency</u>

* Male pattern balding

* <u>Aromatase deficiency</u>

* <u>Hypoandrogenism</u>

* <u>Adrenal insufficiency</u>

* <u>Androgen insensitivity syndrome</u>

* <u>Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism</u> (e.g., <u>Kallman syndrome</u>)

* <u>Hypergonadotropic hypogonadism</u> look (e.g., <u>Klinefelter syndrome</u>)

* <u>5α-reductase deficiency</u>

* <u>17β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase</u> III deficiency

* <u>Ovotesticular disorder of sexual development</u>

* <u>Persistent Mullerian duct syndrome</u>

* <u>46,XY gonadal dysgenesis</u> (<u>Swyer syndrome</u>)

* <u>46,XX testicular disorder of sex development</u>

* For information on drugs influencing the function of the <u>HPG axis</u> and androgens see “<u>Overview of reproductive system drugs</u>.”
